findings.evidence: The document addresses employees directly (line 45: 'You must keep your equipment'), then describes internal staff roles and processes (people operations office, IT asset group, benefits team, managers, finance office) within the same sections without separation. Line 23 explains manager availability issues as if they are relevant applicant information.
findings.fix: Separate content clearly: create distinct sections for applicants vs. internal processes, or add explicit labels like '(For employees)' vs. '(Internal: Benefits Team)' to mark audience switches.
findings.location: Throughout; most acute in 'How to Apply' (line 23) and 'Program Coordination' sections
findings.violation: The document addresses two identifiably different readers - applicants and internal staff - within the same sections without distinguishing which reader each passage targets.

findings.evidence: Eligibility section (lines 11-12): 'If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.' Three conditions are stated before the governing rule.
findings.fix: Reorder to state the main rule first: 'You are eligible for the home-office equipment stipend only if all three of the following conditions are met: (1) your position counts as full-time, (2) you have completed 90 days of continuous service, and (3) your request arrives before the benefit year ends.'
findings.violation: The passage opens with conditions and exceptions (three if-clauses) before stating the governing rule, so a reader must re-read to recover what the benefit actually is.

findings.evidence: The document opens with Program Overview (internal publishing schedule), then covers applicant needs (Eligibility, How to Apply, Timeline), then intersperses internal descriptions (lines 59-61: duplicate Overview; lines 63-65: Program Coordination; lines 67-69: Review Responsibility), breaking the applicant's task sequence.
findings.fix: Move all internal-process sections (Program Coordination, Review Responsibility) to a separate 'For Benefits Team' appendix, or consolidate duplicate Overview sections. Order applicant-facing content by reader task sequence: Eligibility → How to Apply → Required Documentation → Timeline → Reimbursement → Restrictions.
findings.violation: The document's structure mixes internal workflow descriptions with applicant instructions, and includes duplicate sections, so a reader's task sequence is interrupted by internal-process details they do not need.

findings.evidence: 36-word sentence, 4 subordinate-clause markers: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: Terminology Notes section (lines 49-53): The section repeats 'stipend item' three times ('You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review.') without clarifying what 'stipend item' actually refers to or how it differs from other terms used elsewhere.
findings.fix: Either delete this section (applicants do not need internal workflow details) or move it to an internal section with a clear title and opening sentence: 'Internal workflow: How a stipend request moves through the system.' Also define 'stipend item' first: 'A "stipend item" is the specific equipment type you request reimbursement for.'
findings.violation: A reader who has read only this section's first and last sentences cannot state what the section is about, because the section pursues an unexplained internal-process theme ('stipend item' workflow across roles) with no signal of what 'stipend item' actually is or why an applicant should care.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: Terms used interchangeably without definition: 'stipend' vs. 'reimbursement' (lines 5, 11, 13, 39 all describe the same benefit); 'request' vs. 'stipend item' (lines 23, 51 appear to refer to the same artifact). Line 51 repeats 'stipend item' three times without clarifying its meaning.
findings.fix: Choose one term per concept. For example: use 'stipend' consistently (not 'reimbursement'); use 'request' consistently (not 'stipend item'). Add a 'Terminology' section at the start or end that defines each key term once, or add a note like 'This guide uses "request" and "stipend item" to mean the same thing.'
findings.violation: Two or more terms are used interchangeably for identical concepts (stipend/reimbursement, request/stipend item) with no stated equivalence or definition, so a careful reader cannot tell whether the terms name the same thing or distinct steps.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.
